problem: Prior embodied agents store scene or history memory in a single modality (either text or images), which leaves a domain gap between LLM/VLM planning and embodied control, so generated plans are often not executable.
motivation: A good environment memory helps agents remember the scene and produce feasible plans. Text-only memory loses detail, while raw 3D maps are hard for large models to consume. The paper asks how to store richer scene information and whether LLMs and VLMs can cooperate on embodied tasks.
key_idea: Build a Multimodal Environment Memory (object IDs and 3D coordinates as language memory, plus a 2D floor plan projected from a fused point cloud as image memory) that bridges GPT-4/GPT-4V planners and a robot control module.
insight: Combining language memory and image memory gives more executable and precise plans than either alone. Removing MEM hurts instruction-level ESR more than downgrading GPT-4 to GPT-3.5 does (long instructions ESR(a) 15% vs 55%). In embodied QA, removing MEM drops accuracy from 70.0% to 56.7%, and image memory alone without language memory adds little (57.8%).
method: Environmental Language Memory: segmentation image pixels of key items are clustered with K-Means (2 clusters, threshold rule) to get a pixel center, back-projected with depth and intrinsics to camera coordinates, then transformed via extrinsics and the Ginger-to-world frame into world coordinates. Object names/IDs and coordinates are stored as text.

Environmental Image Memory: RGB-D views are turned into colored Open3D point clouds and fused using camera poses. Statistical outlier removal is applied, and the cloud is projected onto the floor plane as a 2D floor plan that shows exploration status.

Embodied Control: a library of encapsulated skills (move to target, make coffee, pour water, grab bread, control AC/curtains/lights, mop, wipe table, straighten chair) that execute the plan using MEM.

Large model division of labor: GPT-3.5 Turbo summarizes dialogue and generates instructions, GPT-4 Turbo decomposes and plans instructions, and GPT-4V handles seating guidance (VLN), spatial dialogue, control guidance and EQA decisions, all through CoT/ICL prompts.

Closed-loop EQA: the model receives the question, MEM and new four-direction observations, plus previously failed plans. It decides whether the information is sufficient, otherwise plans exploration and updates memory, and answers once sufficient.
EQA dataset: GPT-4 Turbo generates random cafe scenes, and question templates (location, comparing, existence) yield 70 scenes and 1050 QA items, manually checked and balanced.

setting.backbone: GPT-4 Turbo / GPT-4V / GPT-3.5 Turbo (frozen, prompted)
setting.observation: egocentric RGB + depth + segmentation images from head/chest/waist cameras
setting.action_space: high-level skill API calls (move to named target, make coffee, wipe table, etc.) and exploration positions
setting.simulator: Dataa Robotics UE5 cafe simulator (Ginger humanoid)
setting.privileged: segmentation images with object IDs are used to build language memory; camera poses are known

numbers.evidence: Table 3: instruction planning evaluation, Short instructions, MEIA row

numbers.eval_set_note: 6 random scenes, 90 questions from the authors' 1050-item dataset; multi-round setting

numbers_note: All benchmarks are the authors' own custom cafe tasks, not standard navigation benchmarks. Full-pipeline ESR of 95% over 20 rounds is given in text only.
results: MEIA reaches 95%/85% instruction ESR on short/long instructions, versus 55%/40% for the strongest baseline Robot-Prompt. GPT-4V scores 98% on VQA and 94% on spatial reasoning versus at most 52% and 38% for open-source VLMs. On EQA, the full model gets 70.0% accuracy, and each memory ablation lowers it.
limitations: Evaluated only in one proprietary simulated cafe with small sample sizes (20 instructions per type, 90 EQA questions); no real robot and no standard benchmarks.
Depends on closed GPT models and privileged segmentation/depth for object coordinates. Spatial reasoning (location questions) remains weak at 55.6%.
Failure cases show planners skip prerequisite steps such as taking a towel.
